title: The first screen of a member community
metaTitle: One object on a community's first screen
excerpt: The first screen of a member community should name one object and one action. A tour makes the post-or-lurk decision for the member. Show the next useful thing and let them do it.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops, a first screen with one object in view and one action to take.
caption: The room is already in session. The first screen should feel the same way. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a member community show?
faqs.answer: Show one real object from the room the person joined, and one action that lets them take part. A thread, a prompt, or the reply they were notified about is enough. A tour, a leaderboard, and a profile checklist can wait until they have posted once. If the room is empty, say so and offer the first post.

faqs.question: Should a new member see a product tour?
faqs.answer: A tour covers the thing they came to see and spends the taps that should have been a reply. Put one line of context beside the object if the object needs it. People who wanted a map can open it later. The first session should end with them having seen a room, not a slideshow about the room.

faqs.question: Where does the home feed belong?
faqs.answer: The home feed belongs after the person has a reason to scan it. If they arrived from an invite to a room or a notification about a reply, open that object. A ranked feed of strangers is a hard first screen, because every post looks like a performance they are late to. Let them reach the feed once they know the tone.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Member community UX, on the first screen, is a single decision: post or lurk. Show the next useful object and one action. Do not open with a tour.

The object is whatever they can respond to right now. A thread. A prompt. A reply that is already waiting. The action is the smallest way to take part, in the words the room already uses. If either is missing, people stay quiet. Quiet can be a choice. A tour that sits on top of the room makes the choice for them.

## The decision this screen is making

A member opens a community for a reason that fits in one sentence. They were invited. They tapped a link in an email. They want to know if they can speak here without performing. The first screen is that test.

Jakob Nielsen, writing for the Nielsen Norman Group, reported that people often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer stay. In a community, the value proposition is not the mission statement. It is proof that there is something to do, and that doing it is small. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the note to keep beside any proposal for a five-step welcome.

They are not choosing your philosophy. They are choosing whether to say something. Lurking is rational. They do not yet know the tone, who is watching, or whether a short reply will notify a hundred people. The screen answers those fears by what it shows.

Show a real object from the room they joined. If the room is empty because the community is new, say so, and make the first post the action. An empty room dressed up as a product tour feels like a lobby with the door locked.

## Name the object in the member's words

Pick one object and name it the way a member would. Thread. Question. Intro. Today's prompt. Do not name it a content item or an activity card. The label is the product.

If they arrived from an invitation to a specific room, that room is the object. Open it. Put the latest useful post in view. If they arrived from a notification about a reply, that reply is the object, and the action is to respond. The home feed is the wrong first screen whenever a specific object brought them in.

When nothing specific brought them, choose the object that helps the decision. A single prompt, with a short field, beats a ranked feed of strangers. A feed can be the second screen. It is a poor first screen for someone who has not spoken, because every post looks finished and theirs would look like an interruption.

Write the name where they can read it without scrolling. On a phone, that is the top of the first view, under a quiet header. The community name can live in the header. It should not be a hero. They already joined.

Use one noun and keep it. If the button says Reply, the success text later should say the reply was posted. A screen that says "Share an update" above a control that says Submit is two products. Pick the sentence the room uses and repeat it in the composer, the button, and the confirmation.

## One action, and no second job

The action is what you want them to do before they decide the place is not for them. Place it on the object. Do not line it up in a toolbar of equal choices.

Reply to this thread. Answer the prompt. Ask a question in this room. Those are good first actions. Complete your profile, invite three people, turn on notifications, read the guidelines, and then post. That list can be real work. None of it should stand in front of the first useful object.

If a rule must be seen before posting, put the one line that changes the decision beside the field. "Posts in this room are visible to every member." A link to the longer code of conduct can sit under it. Do not gate the field behind a checklist they must tick while they are still deciding whether to speak.

The field should look ready. A closed composer that says "Write something" and then opens a different screen is a second product. On the first screen, a single line that expands is enough. The expansion happens because they chose the action, not because a coach mark told them where the button was.

If they cannot post yet, the reason belongs in the interface, in one sentence, where the action would have been. Hiding the action makes the room look broken. A missing reply box is how a new member learns to distrust the product before they have said a word.

## What a tour takes from the first minute

A tour is a sequence of tips laid over the interface. It assumes the person needs a map before they can act. In a community, the room is the map.

Tours fail this screen in ordinary ways. They cover the object. They introduce search, badges, and settings, which matter after someone has posted once. They ask for a tap to dismiss, and that tap is not the action you wanted. The person spends the first 10 seconds learning how to close your help.

If a tour is already built, watch a new member with it turned on. Count the taps before they see a thread they can answer. If the count is more than one, the tour is the product and the community is behind it.

Replace the tour with the object, plus a single line of context when the object is ambiguous. "Ada asked this in Design yesterday" is context. "Step 2 of 4: this is the feed" is a tour. Context sits beside the object. A tour sits on top of it and asks to be forgiven.

Motion that plays before the thread appears spends the same seconds. People who prefer reduced motion should get the thread immediately. So should everyone else. The thread is the point of the screen. A logo animation is a delay dressed up as craft.

## What to leave off this screen

Leave the leaderboard for later. Leave the strip of members they might know. Leave the full list of every room, and leave the prompt to install the app. Those are for someone who has already decided to stay. Here they compete with the action.

Leave the stock scene of people collaborating. It does not name the object. It does not take a reply. It pushes the real thread down, which is the opposite of what a hesitant member needs.

Leave unread counts for rooms they have not chosen. A badge that says 40 makes lurking feel like homework they are already behind on. Show the one room. Let other rooms be a list they open on purpose, after they know what this room sounds like.

Leave profile completion off the banner. A missing photo does not block a short reply. If you need a name, ask for it in the composer at the moment they post. Do not send them to a settings cabinet first. This screen is a room. The cabinet can wait.

If you want the first screen to explain the value, put the value in the object. A specific thread teaches more than a sentence about belonging. Belonging is what they feel after they post and someone answers. You cannot paste that feeling onto an empty hero. You can make the first reply small, and you can make the next response easy to see.

## How to review the screen before you ship

Open a new account on a phone. Do not use the admin account. Admin accounts are full of rooms and powers a member does not have, so they hide the screen you actually shipped.

You should be able to say the object's name and the action's name within a few seconds. If the honest description is "a dashboard," the screen is wrong. If it is "the welcome thread, and I can reply," it is right.

Then try to post something short. If the post fails, the next screen has a different job: say what broke and what to do. That is the piece to read next, [errors in a member community](/blog/errors-in-a-member-community). A first screen that only works on the happy path is unfinished, because the first post is the moment most likely to fail.

When you want to see how a first screen can carry one object and one next step, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The same standard applies here. A stranger should know what the thing is and what to do with it.

Keep four frames in the design file, with real copy, before you call the view done:

- A new member, invited to a room, with one thread to answer
- A new member, empty room, with one honest prompt
- A member returning from a notification, with that object already open
- A member who cannot post yet, with the reason visible where the button would be

If a frame is missing, the first screen is still a guess. The copy is the design. A placeholder that says "Welcome, user" will ship if nobody replaces it on a fresh account, on a phone, before the invite goes out.
